Excerpt is verbatim but is the text as substituted by Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2024 s.2(2)(a); the corpus copy of Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2 shows that between 2022 and 2024 paragraph (a) read 'signed by every executant and attested by a notary public before two witnesses present at the same time', with no authorised-signatory limb, so the researcher's note that this wording is the long-standing content of the section is wrong as stated; the April-2020 wording is not in the corpus and the only corpus support for an authorised signatory at that date is the parallel recital in the unamended 17-1852/s2.

The whole definition of 'power of attorney' was repealed and substituted by Powers of Attorney (Amendment) Act No. 28 of 2022 s.2(1) and substituted again by Act No. 3 of 2024 s.2, and the corpus holds no pre-2022 text, so it cannot be shown from the corpus that the limb relied on, execution before two witnesses and attestation by a notary public, formed part of the definition in April 2020.

Excerpt is verbatim but the corpus consolidation of rule (30) is stale rather than post-2022 as the researcher's note says: 31-2022 s.16(13) substituted the tail of the rule from the words 'he shall preserve a true copy of the registered power of attorney with his protocol' and 6-2024 s.3(10) substituted it again, and neither change is reflected in the corpus text; the April-2020 rule required a copy of the registered power of attorney, while the opening limb relied on, 'If he attest any deed or instrument executed before him by means of an attorney', is untouched by either amendment and was in force at the matter date.

Wording and supporting role are right, but the excerpt quotes 'Form F 1', which 6-2024 s.3(9) substituted for 'Form F', so the excerpt is not the text in force in April 2020 even though the filing duty relied on is.

added_provisions.reason: Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (12) was missing from the map. It is the rule that forbids a notary to attest unless the executant and the witnesses signed in his presence, which is what makes the vendor's inability to travel a legal obstacle at all, and it is the only source of that requirement in the corpus that is temporally stable: no Notaries amendment in the corpus touches rule (12), whereas the presence wording in 7-1840/s2 is 2024 text. Added as indispensable, excerpt checked verbatim.

question_decisions.note: The territorial half of the answer is sound and verified: Notaries Ordinance s.2, s.4A and s.31 rules (12), (22) and (29) all check out verbatim and none of the rules relied on was amended between 1976 and the matter date, so the conclusion that Gayan Alwis cannot attest in Ratnapura and can attest a deed signed in Galle by an attorney holds. The power-of-attorney half does not survive on the corpus at April 2020: 4-1902/s2 and 4-1902/s3 were each repealed and substituted by Act No. 28 of 2022 and the corpus holds no earlier text, and 7-1840/s2 paragraph (a) is 2024 text whose authorised-signatory limb the corpus copy of Act No. 30 of 2022 shows was absent in 2022-2024. Authority requirement is left at statute_only, since the question is in principle answerable from the statute book in force in April 2020, but that statute book is not in the corpus.

disagreements.researcher_position: The corpus text of s.31 rule (30) incorporates the 2022 and 2024 amendments, and the April-2020 rule referred to the registered power of attorney.
disagreements.verifier_position: The corpus consolidation of rule (30) is stale, not current: 31-2022 s.16(13) substituted the tail of the rule from the words 'he shall preserve a true copy of the registered power of attorney with his protocol' and 6-2024 s.3(10) substituted it again, and neither substitution appears in the corpus text, which still reads 'preserve a true copy of the power of attorney with his protocol, and shall forward a like copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands'. The corpus text is therefore older even than the April-2020 rule, which per the words quoted in the 2022 Act required a copy of the registered power of attorney. The opening limb the answer relies on is unaffected either way.

disagreements.researcher_position: The element relied on, that a deed may be signed by the executant or by a person duly authorised by him, is the long-standing content of s.2, so the post-2022 wording can be quoted safely for an April-2020 answer.
disagreements.verifier_position: The corpus copy of Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2 sets out the paragraph (a) it inserted in full, and it contains no authorised-signatory limb; that limb entered the section only through Act No. 4 of 2024 s.2(2)(a). The proposition is probably right for April 2020, since 17-1852/s2 recites the pre-2022 Prevention of Frauds formula and expressly contemplates signature 'by some person lawfully authorized by him', but it cannot be established from the section text the map quotes.

lawyer_questions: What did the definition of 'power of attorney' in s.2 of the Powers of Attorney Ordinance, and s.3 of that Ordinance, say in April 2020, before Act No. 28 of 2022 repealed and substituted both? Specifically, did the pre-2022 definition itself require execution before two witnesses and attestation by a notary public, or did that requirement come from the general law? The whole power-of-attorney method, and therefore the answer to the second half of the question, turns on this.
Confirm the April-2020 text of Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, in particular whether it permitted signature by a person lawfully authorised by the executant, as 17-1852/s2 implies.
Confirm that Ratnapura lies outside the judicial zone covered by a Galle High Court warrant; the corpus holds no instrument fixing zone boundaries.

Is execution before a District Judge or a specially authorised Justice of the Peace under the Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance No. 17 of 1852 still a live route in practice, or should the gold answer's second method be confined to attestation by a notary holding a warrant for the Ratnapura zone?
